videos.caption: Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

Humanoid robotics in one clip: one robot standing, another flat on the floor while engineers rush in. This is what real hardware development looks like. Balance, fall recovery, joint control and whole-body coordination still have to survive outside controlled lab demos. Every failure exposes something engineers can improve. #HumanoidRobot #HumanoidRobotics #PhysicalAI #EmbodiedAI #Robotics

A humanoid robot was blasted in the chest and still stayed on its feet. This viral video appears to show two armored humanoid robots being struck by rounds claimed to be from a 20 mm cannon. Sparks, smoke, and debris fly as the machines absorb the impacts, yet neither one collapses. If authentic, it could offer a disturbing glimpse into the future of military robotics: machines designed not only to walk and work, but also to survive dangerous combat environments. However, the video does not identify the manufacturer, testing organization, or location, and the claims have not been independently verified. Impressive engineering, clever visual effects, or an early look at future warfare? Would robots like these make soldiers safer, or make warfare even more dangerous?
